title: Test Prep: SAT · ACT · ASVAB
description: A focused review course for the SAT, ACT, and ASVAB that builds the algebra, geometry, reading, and grammar skills shared across all three exams, plus the strategy, pacing, and answer-elimination habits that turn content knowledge into a higher score. The final unit covers the ASVAB's unique technical sections, the AFQT formula, and how to handle test-day logistics and nerves.
outcomes: You can describe how the SAT, ACT, and ASVAB are each scored and structured, and pace yourself to finish every section with time to check your work.
You can eliminate wrong answer choices using test-maker patterns even on questions where you don't immediately know the right answer.
You can solve the linear equation, percentage, exponent, quadratic, and geometry problems that make up the bulk of every test's math section.
You can fix run-ons, agreement errors, and parallelism mistakes, and read a passage for structure and command of evidence.
You can reason through mechanical comprehension and electronics questions, and calculate what feeds into your ASVAB AFQT score.
You can build a realistic study schedule and manage test-day logistics and anxiety so your prep actually shows up in your score.

units.title: How These Tests Actually Work
units.summary: The structure, scoring, and pacing habits shared across the SAT, ACT, and ASVAB, plus how to read wrong answers as deliberately designed traps.

lessons.title: SAT, ACT, and ASVAB at a Glance
lessons.intro: Walk into the wrong test assuming it works like the one your older sibling took, and you'll waste minutes relearning the format instead of answering questions. The SAT, ACT, and ASVAB test overlapping skills, but they're built differently, scored differently, and reward different habits, so the first strategy for any of them is simply knowing the shape of the thing in front of you.

sections.heading: What Each Test Is Actually For
body: The SAT and ACT are college-admissions tests; colleges use your score alongside grades and essays to decide admission and sometimes scholarships. The Digital SAT has two scored sections, Reading and Writing, then Math, scored 200-800 each for a combined 400-1600. It's computer-adaptive: your performance on the first half of a section decides whether the second half is easier or harder, which changes your score more than the raw number of questions you get right.

The ACT covers English, Math, and Reading as its required sections, with Science offered as an optional fourth; your Composite score (1-36) averages the three required sections, and Science only factors in if you choose to report it. The ASVAB is different in kind, it's a military enlistment and job-placement test with subjects like Arithmetic Reasoning, Word Knowledge, and Mechanical Comprehension, and it doesn't just gate admission, it determines which military jobs you qualify for.

sections.heading: Same Skills, Different Packaging
body: All three tests draw on the same underlying skills: reading closely, doing algebra and geometry without a wobble, and writing or recognizing correct grammar. If you're prepping for more than one, that overlap means algebra practice for the SAT also sharpens you for the ASVAB's Mathematics Knowledge section, you're not starting from zero on each.

What differs is the packaging: the SAT rewards efficient reading of shorter passages and rewards accuracy over speed since it's adaptive; the ACT is not adaptive and simply has less time per question, so pace matters more; the ASVAB has more standalone sections, like Electronics Information, that test knowledge you either have or don't, rather than reasoning you can work out on the spot.

keyTerms.def: The ACT's average of English, Math, and Reading scores (1-36), the number colleges see unless Science is also reported.
A format (used by the Digital SAT) where your accuracy on an early module determines the difficulty, and therefore the scoring ceiling, of the next module.
Armed Forces Qualification Test score, the ASVAB composite that determines basic eligibility to enlist.

practice.q: Which statement correctly describes the Digital SAT's scoring?
choices: It scores 1-36 based on four required sections
It's computer-adaptive with a 400-1600 combined score from two sections
It only reports a single combined score with no section breakdown
It's scored the same as the ASVAB's AFQT
practice.explain: The SAT is adaptive and has two scored sections (Reading and Writing, and Math), each worth 200-800, combining to 400-1600. The 1-36 scale and four-section structure describes the ACT, not the SAT.

practice.q: A student is deciding whether to also report their ACT Science score. Which is true?
choices: Science always counts toward the Composite whether reported or not
The Composite only averages English, Math, and Reading; Science is optional and separate
Science replaces the Reading section in the Composite
The ACT no longer offers a Science section at all
practice.explain: Under the current ACT format, Science is an optional fourth section. The Composite is the average of the three required sections (English, Math, Reading) regardless of whether a student also takes and reports Science.

practice.q: Why does the ASVAB matter beyond a simple pass/fail?
choices: It only affects whether you can retake the test
It has no connection to specific jobs, only overall eligibility
Line scores built from its subtests determine which military jobs you qualify for
It replaces the need for a high school diploma
practice.explain: Beyond the AFQT eligibility score, the ASVAB's individual subtest scores combine into line scores used to match recruits to specific military occupational specialties.

lessons.title: Pacing, Time Management, and the Guessing Question
lessons.intro: Running out of time on a section you actually know the content for is one of the most preventable ways to lose points on these tests, and it happens constantly, because pacing has to be practiced separately from content.

sections.heading: Building a Pace, Not Just Watching the Clock
body: Divide the time in a section by the number of questions to get a per-question budget, then build in a buffer. On the Digital SAT's Math module, roughly 44 questions in 70 minutes gives about 1.6 minutes each; on the ACT's English section, 50 questions in 35 minutes gives closer to 40 seconds each. Knowing that number before you sit down changes how you behave at question 12 when you're stuck: you flag it and move on rather than losing five minutes you don't have.

A practical habit is checking in at fixed checkpoints instead of watching every second, for a 40-question section, glance at the clock after question 10, 20, and 30, and compare your position to where the raw pace says you should be. If you're behind at checkpoint one, that's a signal to speed up on easier questions, not to panic and rush the rest of the section.

sections.heading: Guessing: No Penalty, Big Difference
body: Both the SAT and ACT score only correct answers, there's no point deducted for a wrong guess, so an unanswered question and a wrong guess cost you the same, but a lucky guess costs you nothing. That single fact means you should never leave a bubble blank: with four or five answer choices, a blind guess still has a 20-25% chance of paying off, and eliminating even one choice improves those odds further.

The ASVAB works the same way, no penalty for incorrect answers, but it's worth budgeting your last minute in any timed subtest to fill in every remaining bubble with a single letter rather than leaving several blank, since a consistent guess pattern statistically nets you some free points that random last-second guessing might not.

keyTerms.def: Total section time divided by number of questions, used to set a pacing target before you start.
Comparing your progress at fixed intervals (like question 10, 20, 30) against your target pace, rather than watching the clock continuously.
A scoring method (used by the SAT, ACT, and ASVAB) that counts only correct answers, so guessing carries no penalty.

practice.q: On a 60-question section with 45 minutes, roughly how much time should you budget per question?
choices: 30 seconds
45 seconds
75 seconds
90 seconds
practice.explain: 45 minutes equals 2,700 seconds; 2,700 divided by 60 questions is 45 seconds per question.

practice.q: With 10 minutes left and 8 unanswered multiple-choice questions (4 choices each) on a rights-only-scored test, what's the best move?
choices: Leave them blank since guessing is risky
Guess the same letter for all 8 to guarantee some correct answers
Skip ahead and only answer questions you're fully sure about
Spend all 10 minutes rereading the passage instead
practice.explain: Since wrong answers aren't penalized, filling in a single consistent letter across remaining questions is better than leaving them blank, statistically you'll get roughly 1 in 4 correct for free, and blanks guarantee zero.

practice.q: Why is checkpoint pacing more useful than constantly watching the clock?
choices: It eliminates the need to know the total time limit
It tells you whether you're on pace at specific moments without constant distraction, so you can adjust before it's too late
It only works on adaptive tests like the SAT
It guarantees you'll finish every question correctly
practice.explain: Checking your position against target pace at a few fixed points gives you actionable information (speed up, or you're fine) without the distraction and anxiety of watching the clock every few seconds.

lessons.title: Reading Like a Test-Maker: Process of Elimination
lessons.intro: Wrong answers on these tests aren't random, they're written on purpose to look tempting, and once you recognize the handful of patterns test-makers reuse, you can eliminate two or three choices on questions where you don't even know the right answer yet.

sections.heading: The Trap Patterns
body: The most common trap is the half-right answer: a choice that correctly restates part of the passage or problem but adds a detail, a scope, or a conclusion the source doesn't support. Another is the extreme-language answer, using words like 'always,' 'never,' or 'proves,' which is rarely justified by a passage that hedges with words like 'often' or 'suggests.' A third is the right-answer-wrong-question trap, where a choice is true and even appears in the passage, but doesn't actually answer what was asked.

On math sections, a frequent trap is the answer you'd get from one common mistake, for instance, forgetting to distribute a negative sign, or computing a percentage of the wrong base number. Test-makers deliberately include these as wrong-choice options because they know which errors students make most often, which is exactly why checking your work against the actual question, not just re-doing the arithmetic, catches these.

sections.heading: Eliminate Before You Confirm
body: Instead of hunting for the right answer first, read all four choices and cross out anything that's factually wrong, off-topic, or uses extreme language unsupported by the passage. Doing this even when you're unsure narrows a blind guess from 1-in-4 to 1-in-2, which is a meaningfully better outcome under time pressure.

Once you're down to two choices, go back to the specific line or sentence in the passage, or redo the specific step in a math problem, that the question is actually about, rather than relying on a vague feeling that one choice sounds right. The choice that survives a direct check against the source text or your work is the answer; the one that only sounded plausible is the trap.

keyTerms.def: An answer choice that's correct in part but adds an unsupported detail or wrong scope.
A wrong choice using absolute words ('always,' 'never,' 'proves') that the source material doesn't actually support.
Systematically ruling out clearly wrong choices to improve your odds before selecting or guessing.

practice.q: A passage says a policy 'sometimes reduced costs for small businesses.' Which answer choice is most likely a trap?
choices: The policy occasionally lowered costs for small businesses
The policy reduced costs for small businesses in some cases
The policy always reduced costs for all businesses
The policy had a mixed effect on small business costs
practice.explain: 'Always' and 'all' are extreme language the passage doesn't support, it says 'sometimes' and specifies small businesses, not all businesses.

practice.q: You solve a percent-decrease problem and your answer matches a choice exactly, but the question actually asked for a percent increase. What should you do?
choices: Pick that answer since it matches a choice exactly
Recheck which operation the question actually asked for before selecting
Assume the test made an error
Switch to a completely different problem-solving method
practice.explain: Matching a choice exactly is a classic sign you may have solved for the wrong thing, a common trap is including the answer to the 'almost-question' as a wrong choice. Always verify against what was actually asked.

practice.q: What's the main benefit of eliminating clearly wrong choices before trying to confirm the right one?
choices: It guarantees you'll never need to guess
It narrows your odds on a guess and often reveals the right answer by contrast
It saves time by letting you skip reading the passage
It only helps on reading questions, not math
practice.explain: Elimination improves guessing odds and often makes the correct answer clearer once the traps are removed, and it works on both reading and math sections.

units.title: Reading and Language Skills
units.summary: Reading passages for structure and evidence, decoding vocabulary in and out of context, and fixing the grammar errors these tests test most.

lessons.title: Reading for Structure and Evidence
lessons.intro: Rereading a passage three times because you can't remember what it said wastes exactly the time you don't have, the fix is reading once, but reading for the right things: what the passage is doing, not just what it's saying.

sections.heading: Find the Job of Each Paragraph
body: Every well-constructed passage has paragraphs that each do a job: introduce a claim, provide evidence, complicate the claim, or conclude. As you read, jot a three-to-five word label next to each paragraph, 'intro,' 'example,' 'counter,' 'wrap-up,' rather than trying to memorize every detail. This turns a dense passage into a map you can scan back to when a question asks where a specific idea appears.

This matters because most reading questions aren't really about small details, they're about structure and function: why the author included a specific example, how paragraph three relates to paragraph two, or what the passage's main claim is. A reader who tracked structure while reading can answer these in seconds; a reader who only absorbed content has to reread and hunt.

sections.heading: Command of Evidence: Prove It From the Text
body: A large share of reading questions ask you to identify which line or sentence best supports an answer to the previous question, sometimes called command of evidence. The trick is to answer the content question first using your own understanding, then treat the evidence question as a lookup task: find the specific sentence that states or directly implies that answer, not just a sentence that's topically related.

A common error is picking an evidence line that's about the right topic but doesn't actually prove the specific claim being tested. If a question asks what evidence shows a policy was unpopular, a line describing the policy's goals is topically related but doesn't prove unpopularity, you need the line that actually mentions opposition, protest, or declining support.

keyTerms.def: Labeling each paragraph's function (intro, example, counter, conclusion) while reading to build a quick mental map of the passage.
A question type asking which specific line or sentence best supports a previous answer.
An evidence choice that mentions the right subject but doesn't actually prove the specific claim in question.

practice.q: A passage's third paragraph opens with 'Critics, however, argued that...' What is this paragraph's most likely job?
choices: Introducing the passage's main topic
Providing a counterargument or complication to an earlier claim
Summarizing the entire passage
Defining a technical term used later
practice.explain: 'However' signals a shift, and 'critics argued' introduces an opposing view, this paragraph is complicating or countering a claim made earlier, not introducing or summarizing.

practice.q: A question asks which line best shows a new policy faced public opposition. Which type of line should you select?
choices: A line explaining the policy's original goals
A line describing who proposed the policy
A line that specifically mentions protests, declining approval, or public criticism
A line defining a related but different policy
practice.explain: The evidence must directly support the specific claim (opposition), not just be topically connected to the policy in general.

practice.q: What's the main advantage of labeling each paragraph's function while reading?
choices: It lets you skip reading half the passage
It builds a quick map you can scan instead of rereading for structure questions
It's required by the test format
It replaces the need to understand vocabulary
practice.explain: Structure mapping saves time on structure and function questions by giving you a scannable map instead of forcing a full reread.

lessons.title: Vocabulary in Context and Word Knowledge
lessons.intro: These tests almost never ask for a dictionary definition in isolation, they ask what a word means right there, in that sentence, which means the same word can have a different correct answer on different questions.

sections.heading: Words Change Meaning With Context
body: Take the word 'temper.' In 'she tempered her criticism with encouragement,' temper means to soften or moderate. In 'he lost his temper,' temper means anger. A vocabulary-in-context question will give you a sentence and ask which definition fits that specific use, picking the most common meaning of a word instead of the meaning that fits the sentence is the single most frequent error on this question type.

The reliable method is to cover the answer choices, read the sentence, and predict a simple substitute word in your own words first, for 'tempered her criticism,' you might predict 'softened' or 'balanced.' Then match your prediction to the closest choice, rather than reading the choices first and letting a familiar-looking word pull you toward its most common meaning.

sections.heading: Word Knowledge Without Full Sentences (ASVAB-Style)
body: The ASVAB's Word Knowledge section often tests a word with little or no context, either asking for a synonym directly or a one-line usage. Here, the fix is building real vocabulary rather than relying on context clues that won't be there, but you can still narrow choices using word roots and parts: 'loquacious' contains the Latin root 'loqu-' (to speak), pointing toward 'talkative,' not 'quiet' or 'angry.'

A practical study method is grouping words by root or prefix rather than memorizing an alphabetical list: 'bene-' (good, as in benevolent, beneficial), 'mal-' (bad, as in malicious, malfunction), '-ology' (study of). Roots let you make an educated guess on unfamiliar words instead of guessing blind, which matters because Word Knowledge questions rarely give you a sentence to lean on.

keyTerms.def: A question type asking what a word means specifically within a given sentence, not its most common dictionary definition.
Reading a sentence, predicting your own substitute word, then finding the closest matching answer choice.
A core word part (like 'loqu-' for speech, 'bene-' for good) that hints at meaning even without full sentence context.

practice.q: In the sentence 'The committee's report was measured, avoiding any sweeping claims,' what does 'measured' most nearly mean?
choices: Physically sized with instruments
Cautious and carefully restrained
Extremely aggressive
Randomly assembled
practice.explain: In context, 'measured' describes a careful, restrained tone (paired with 'avoiding sweeping claims'), not a physical measurement.

practice.q: Given the root 'mal-' means 'bad,' which word most likely means 'to work badly or incorrectly'?
choices: Malfunction
Benefit
Loquacious
Credible
practice.explain: 'Mal-' (bad) plus 'function' gives 'malfunction,' to function badly. The other words use unrelated or opposite roots.

practice.q: What is the biggest risk of reading answer choices before predicting your own substitute word?
choices: It takes too much extra time either way
A familiar-looking word can pull you toward its most common meaning instead of the contextual one
It's not allowed by test rules
It only matters for math questions
practice.explain: Predicting first anchors you to the sentence's actual meaning; reading choices first lets a common definition bias your choice even when it doesn't fit the context.

lessons.title: Grammar and Sentence Construction
lessons.intro: The English and Writing sections aren't testing whether you can recite grammar rules, they're testing whether you can spot the one thing wrong with a sentence in about 30 seconds, which is a different and very learnable skill.

sections.heading: Fragments, Run-ons, and Comma Splices
body: A sentence needs at least one independent clause, a subject and verb that could stand alone. 'Running to catch the bus' is a fragment because it has no subject doing a complete action. A run-on jams two independent clauses together with no punctuation: 'The exam was hard I still finished early.' A comma splice is almost right but uses only a comma to join two independent clauses: 'The exam was hard, I still finished early,' a comma alone isn't strong enough to join them.

There are several correct fixes, and the test usually offers more than one in the choices: add a coordinating conjunction after the comma ('The exam was hard, but I still finished early'), use a semicolon ('The exam was hard; I still finished early'), or split it into two sentences. Recognizing which fix a specific question wants often comes down to matching the tone and conjunction meaning ('but' for contrast, 'so' for result) to what the sentence is actually saying.

example.problem: Fix this run-on sentence: 'The lab results came back late the team had to revise their conclusions.'
steps: Identify the two independent clauses: 'the lab results came back late' and 'the team had to revise their conclusions.'
Notice these are joined with no punctuation at all, that's a run-on.
Choose a fix that matches the logical relationship: the second clause is a result of the first, so 'so' fits better than 'but.'
Join with a comma plus the coordinating conjunction: 'The lab results came back late, so the team had to revise their conclusions.'
example.answer: The lab results came back late, so the team had to revise their conclusions.

sections.heading: Agreement, Pronouns, and Parallel Structure
body: Subject-verb agreement means the verb must match its actual subject, even when other words sit in between. In 'the box of tools was heavy,' the subject is 'box' (singular), not 'tools,' so 'was' is correct even though 'tools' sits right before the verb. Pronoun agreement works the same way: formal written English often prefers matching number, as in 'each student must bring his or her own laptop,' or rewriting the sentence in the plural, 'students must bring their own laptops.'

Parallel structure means items in a list or comparison should use matching grammatical form. 'She enjoys hiking, swimming, and to read' breaks parallelism because the first two items are gerunds ('-ing' words) and the third switches to an infinitive ('to read'). The fix matches all three: 'hiking, swimming, and reading.' Test questions often bury this error in a longer sentence specifically so the mismatch is easy to miss on a fast read.

keyTerms.def: A group of words with a subject and verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence.
Errors that join two independent clauses with no punctuation, or with only a comma, when stronger punctuation or a conjunction is needed.
Matching grammatical form across items in a list or comparison (all gerunds, all infinitives, etc.).

practice.q: Which sentence corrects the following comma splice? 'The report was late, the client grew frustrated.'
choices: The report was late the client grew frustrated.
The report was late, and the client grew frustrated.
The report, was late, the client grew frustrated.
The report was late the, client grew frustrated.
practice.explain: Adding a coordinating conjunction ('and') after the comma correctly joins the two independent clauses. The original only had a comma, which isn't strong enough on its own.

practice.q: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
choices: The list of ingredients are on the counter.
The list of ingredients is on the counter.
The list of ingredients were on the counter.
The lists of ingredients is on the counter.
practice.explain: The subject is 'list' (singular), not 'ingredients,' so the singular verb 'is' is correct despite the plural noun sitting closer to the verb.

practice.q: Which version fixes the parallelism error in 'The manager wanted to cut costs, improving morale, and to expand the team'?
choices: The manager wanted to cut costs, to improve morale, and to expand the team.
The manager wanted cutting costs, improving morale, and to expand the team.
The manager wanted to cut costs, improve morale, expanding the team.
No change is needed.
practice.explain: All three items need matching form. Using the infinitive 'to' consistently ('to cut,' 'to improve,' 'to expand') fixes the mismatch created by 'improving' in the middle.

practice.q: What makes 'Running late to the meeting' a fragment rather than a complete sentence?
choices: It's too short to be a sentence
It has no subject performing a complete action with a finite verb
It doesn't end with a period
It uses the wrong verb tense
practice.explain: A fragment lacks an independent clause, here there's no subject paired with a complete, standalone verb; 'running' is acting like a description, not a main verb making a complete statement.

units.title: Math Core: Algebra and Word Problems
units.summary: Solving linear equations, percentages, exponents, radicals, and quadratics, and translating word problems into equations you can actually solve.

lessons.title: Linear Equations, Ratios, and Percentages
lessons.intro: Roughly a third of the math questions on these tests boil down to solving a linear equation or working a percentage, which means getting these fast and error-free is the single highest-leverage math skill you can build.

sections.heading: Solving Linear Equations Cleanly
body: A linear equation is solved by isolating the variable using inverse operations, applied to both sides in the same order every time: undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division, and distribute before combining like terms. Rushing the order, or distributing incorrectly, is where most errors happen, not in some advanced step, but in basic arithmetic done too fast.

Writing out each step, even ones that feel obvious, catches errors before they compound. On a timed test this feels slower, but a clean two-line solution that's right beats a mental shortcut that's wrong and forces a restart.

sections.heading: Percent Change: Watch the Base
body: A percentage is always a percentage of something, the base, and the most common percent error is applying a percentage to the wrong base, especially with sequential discounts. A 25% discount followed by a 10% discount is not a 35% total discount, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price, not the original.

The reliable method is to convert each percentage to a decimal multiplier and multiply straight through. A 25% discount means you pay 75% (0.75) of the price; a further 10% off means you then pay 90% (0.90) of that. Multiplying the multipliers together (0.75 x 0.90 = 0.675) tells you immediately that the combined effect is paying 67.5% of the original price, a 32.5% total discount, not 35%.

example.problem: A jacket costs $40. It's marked down 25%, then an additional 10% off the sale price. What's the final price?
steps: First discount: $40 x 0.75 = $30 (paying 75% after a 25% markdown)
Second discount applies to the new price: $30 x 0.90 = $27
Final price is $27, not $40 x 0.65 = $26, sequential discounts don't simply add.

keyTerms.def: Operations that undo each other (addition/subtraction, multiplication/division), used in order to isolate a variable.
The quantity a percentage is calculated from, critical to identify correctly, especially in multi-step or sequential percent problems.
Converting a percent change (like a 25% decrease) into a single multiplying factor (0.75) to simplify percent calculations.

practice.q: Solve for x: 5x + 8 = 2x - 4
practice.explain: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x + 8 = -4. Subtract 8: 3x = -12. Divide by 3: x = -4.

practice.q: A phone originally costs $200. It's discounted 20%, then the store takes an additional 15% off the new price. What is the final price?
practice.explain: $200 x 0.80 = $160 after the first discount. $160 x 0.85 = $136 after the second. Applying 35% off $200 directly ($130) is the sequential-discount trap and is incorrect.

practice.q: If a value increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%, what happens to the original value?
choices: It returns exactly to the original value
It ends up lower than the original value
It ends up higher than the original value
It's impossible to determine
practice.explain: Multiplying by 1.20 then 0.80 gives 0.96 of the original, a net 4% decrease, because the 20% decrease is applied to a larger number than the 20% increase was.

practice.q: Solve for x: 2(x + 3) - 4 = 3x - 1
practice.explain: Distribute: 2x + 6 - 4 = 3x - 1, so 2x + 2 = 3x - 1. Subtract 2x: 2 = x - 1. Add 1: x = 3.

lessons.title: Exponents, Radicals, and Quadratics
lessons.intro: Quadratics show up constantly disguised as area problems, projectile-motion word problems, and standalone algebra, and nearly all of them factor cleanly enough to solve by hand in under a minute once you know the pattern.

sections.heading: Exponent Rules That Actually Get Tested
body: The rules that matter most are: multiplying same-base powers adds exponents (x^3^ x x^2^ = x^5^), dividing same-base powers subtracts exponents (x^5^ / x^2^ = x^3^), and raising a power to a power multiplies exponents ((x^2^)^3^ = x^6^). A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: x^-2^ = 1/x^2^, not a negative number.

Radicals follow similar logic: √(a x b) = √a x √b, which lets you simplify √50 by splitting it into √25 x √2 = 5√2. A common mistake is assuming √(a+b) equals √a + √b, this is false in general (√(9+16) = √25 = 5, but √9 + √16 = 3+4 = 7), so radicals only split cleanly over multiplication and division, never over addition or subtraction.

sections.heading: Factoring Quadratics to Solve for x
body: A quadratic in the form x^2^ + bx + c = 0 factors into two binomials (x + m)(x + n) where m x n = c and m + n = b. To solve x^2^ - 5x - 14 = 0, look for two numbers that multiply to -14 and add to -5: those are -7 and 2, giving (x - 7)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 7 or x = -2.

When a quadratic won't factor with nice integers, the quadratic formula x = (-b +/- √(b^2^-4ac)) / 2a always works, using a, b, and c from the standard form ax^2^ + bx + c = 0. It's slower than factoring, so try factoring first (numbers that multiply and add cleanly), but the formula is the reliable fallback when the factors aren't whole numbers.

steps: Find two numbers that multiply to -14 and add to -5: -7 and 2 work (-7 x 2 = -14, -7 + 2 = -5).
Set each factor to zero: x - 7 = 0 or x + 2 = 0

keyTerms.def: Multiply same-base powers by adding exponents, divide by subtracting exponents, and raise a power to a power by multiplying exponents.
Breaking a radical into a perfect-square factor and a remaining factor, valid only across multiplication/division, not addition/subtraction.
x = (-b +/- √(b^2^-4ac)) / 2a, which solves any quadratic ax^2^+bx+c=0 even when it doesn't factor with whole numbers.

practice.q: Simplify: x^4^ x x^3^
practice.explain: Multiplying same-base powers adds the exponents: 4 + 3 = 7, giving x^7^.

practice.q: Simplify √72
practice.explain: 72 = 36 x 2, and √36 = 6, so √72 = 6√2. (2√18 is equal in value but not simplified, 18 still has a perfect-square factor.)

practice.q: Solve x^2^ + 2x - 15 = 0
choices: x = 5 or x = -3
x = -5 or x = 3
x = 3 or x = 5
x = -3 or x = -5
practice.explain: Two numbers that multiply to -15 and add to 2 are 5 and -3 (5 x -3 = -15, 5 + -3 = 2), giving factors (x+5)(x-3)=0, so x = -5 or x = 3.

practice.q: Which expression is equivalent to √a + √b for positive a and b?
choices: It cannot generally be simplified to a single radical
√a x √b
practice.explain: Unlike multiplication, radicals do not distribute over addition, √a + √b is not equal to √(a+b) in general, as shown by √9+√16=7 versus √25=5.

lessons.title: Translating Word Problems into Equations
lessons.intro: The hardest part of most word problems isn't the math, it's translation. Once English sentences become an equation, solving is usually the easy part; the skill worth practicing is turning phrases like 'the cost was reduced by' into the correct expression.

sections.heading: Translating Key Phrases
body: Certain words reliably map to certain operations: 'sum,' 'total,' 'combined,' and 'more than' signal addition; 'difference' and 'less than' signal subtraction (careful with order, '5 less than x' is x - 5, not 5 - x); 'product,' 'times,' and 'of' (in percentage contexts) signal multiplication; 'quotient,' 'per,' and 'divided among' signal division.

Order matters most with subtraction and division phrases. 'The cost was reduced by $15' translates to (original cost) - 15, while 'reduced to $15' would instead mean the new value equals 15 directly, small wording differences change the entire setup, so read the sentence for exactly what changes and what stays fixed.

sections.heading: Setting Up a Full Word Problem
body: Start by naming your unknown clearly, 'let m = number of miles,' rather than jumping straight to symbols. Then convert each piece of information into an expression using that variable, and finally set those expressions equal to the total or constraint given in the problem. Writing the setup in words first (total cost equals flat fee plus per-mile rate times miles) before converting to symbols catches translation errors early.

After solving, always check the answer against the original scenario, not just the equation, if a word problem about people yields a negative or fractional person, you've mistranslated something, even if the algebra itself was done correctly.

example.problem: A car rental company charges a flat fee of $35 plus $0.20 per mile. If a customer's budget is $75, how many miles can they drive?
steps: Let m = number of miles driven.

keyTerms.def: Words (sum, difference, product, quotient, per, less than) that reliably map to specific mathematical operations.
A phrase like '5 less than x' (= x - 5) where reversing the order changes the meaning of the expression.
Verifying a solved answer makes sense in the real-world context of the problem, not just that the algebra was executed correctly.

practice.q: Translate: '8 less than twice a number n'
practice.explain: 'Twice a number' is 2n; '8 less than' that means subtracting 8 from it afterward: 2n - 8, not 8 - 2n.

practice.q: A gym charges a $30 signup fee plus $25 per month. Which equation gives total cost C after m months?
practice.explain: The fixed fee ($30) is added once; the monthly rate ($25) multiplies by the number of months m: C = 25m + 30.

practice.q: Solving a word problem about the number of buses needed for a field trip, you get x = 4.6. What should you do?
choices: Report 4.6 buses as the final answer
Round down to 4, since a partial bus can't be used
Round up to 5, since 4 buses wouldn't hold everyone
Conclude the problem has no valid solution
practice.explain: A sanity check matters here: you can't dispatch a fractional bus, and rounding down would leave people without transportation, so you round up to the next whole bus even though 4.6 rounds down mathematically.

practice.q: Which phrase translates to division?
choices: The sum of x and y
The product of x and y
x divided among 4 people
x more than y
practice.explain: 'Divided among' signals division (x / 4). 'Sum' signals addition, 'product' signals multiplication, and 'more than' signals addition.

units.title: Math Core: Geometry, Data, and Science Reasoning
units.summary: Triangle and circle formulas, reading graphs and statistics correctly, and the reasoning skills tested by the ACT's Science section and the ASVAB's General Science subtest.

lessons.title: Geometry Essentials: Angles, Triangles, and Circles
lessons.intro: Geometry questions reward knowing a small set of formulas cold rather than rederiving them under pressure, the Pythagorean theorem, triangle angle sum, and circle formulas alone cover the large majority of geometry questions on these tests.

sections.heading: Triangles and the Pythagorean Theorem
body: The interior angles of any triangle always sum to 180°, which lets you find a missing angle immediately if you know the other two. For right triangles specifically, the Pythagorean theorem a^2^ + b^2^ = c^2^ relates the two legs (a, b) to the hypotenuse (c, the side opposite the right angle), and recognizing common triples like 3-4-5 and 6-8-10 (3-4-5 doubled) saves time versus computing square roots from scratch.

Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional sides, which is the basis for many shadow or ramp word problems: if a 6-foot person casts a 4-foot shadow at the same time a flagpole casts a 20-foot shadow, the ratio 6/4 equals height/20, giving a height of 30 feet.

example.problem: A right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.
steps: Apply the Pythagorean theorem: a^2^ + b^2^ = c^2^

sections.heading: Circles: Area and Circumference
body: A circle's circumference (distance around) is C = 2πr or πd, and its area is A = πr^2^, where r is the radius. The most common error is mixing up which formula uses radius squared and which uses just radius or diameter, area needs the radius squared because it measures a two-dimensional space, while circumference is a one-dimensional length.

Many test questions give the diameter, not the radius, expecting you to divide by 2 first, plugging the diameter directly into A = πr^2^ instead of halving it first is a frequent, entirely avoidable error, so always confirm which measurement you were actually given before using a formula.

example.problem: A circular garden has a diameter of 10 meters. Find its area, in terms of π.
steps: Find the radius: r = diameter / 2 = 10 / 2 = 5 meters
Apply the area formula: A = πr^2^

keyTerms.def: a^2^+b^2^=c^2^, relating a right triangle's two legs to its hypotenuse.
Triangles with equal corresponding angles and proportional sides, used to solve indirect-measurement problems.
The radius is half the diameter; area formulas use radius squared, so a given diameter must be halved first.

practice.q: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
practice.explain: 9^2^+12^2^ = 81+144 = 225, and √225 = 15. (This is the 3-4-5 triple scaled by 3.)

practice.q: A triangle has two known angles of 50° and 70°. What is the third angle?
practice.explain: Triangle angles sum to 180°; 180 - 50 - 70 = 60°.

practice.q: A circle has a radius of 4 cm. What is its circumference in terms of π?
choices: 4π cm
8π cm
16π cm
2π cm
practice.explain: C = 2πr = 2π(4) = 8π cm.

practice.q: A circle's diameter is 14 inches. Using A = πr^2^, what is its area in terms of π?
choices: 196π in²
49π in²
14π in²
98π in²
practice.explain: Radius = diameter / 2 = 7 inches. A = π(7)^2^ = 49π square inches. Using the diameter directly instead of the radius (giving 196π) is the common error this question is testing.

lessons.title: Reading Graphs, Tables, and Statistics
lessons.intro: A surprising number of points on these tests don't require solving anything, they require correctly reading a graph or table, and a surprising number of students lose those points anyway by misreading an axis or grabbing the wrong row.

sections.heading: Reading Axes, Scales, and Trends Correctly
body: Before reading any data off a graph, check both axes: what units they're in, whether the scale is linear or something else, and whether it starts at zero. A bar graph with a y-axis starting at 80 instead of 0 can make a small difference look dramatic, which is a common way real-world data, and test questions, can mislead a fast reader.

For a line graph, the slope between two points tells you the rate of change, not the value at either point, a common wrong-answer trap asks you to read off the final value when the question actually asked how much something changed over an interval, or vice versa. Always reread the question after finding a number on the graph to confirm you found what was actually asked.

sections.heading: Mean, Median, and Percent Change
body: The mean (average) is the sum of values divided by the count; the median is the middle value when data is sorted (or the average of the two middle values if the count is even). For the set {2, 4, 4, 6, 9}, the mean is (2+4+4+6+9)/5 = 25/5 = 5, while the median is the middle (third) value once sorted, which is 4, the two measures often differ, especially when one value is unusually large or small (an outlier), which pulls the mean but not the median.

Percent change is calculated as (new value - old value) / old value x 100. If a company's sales went from 240 units to 300 units, the percent change is (300-240)/240 x 100 = 60/240 x 100 = 25%. Using the new value as the denominator instead of the old value is a common and completely avoidable error.

example.problem: A store's monthly sales rose from 240 units to 300 units. What is the percent increase?

keyTerms.def: The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle value of sorted data, outliers affect the mean much more than the median.
A value much higher or lower than the rest of a data set, which can pull the mean away from where most of the data actually sits.
(new - old) / old x 100, always using the original value as the denominator.

practice.q: Find the mean of the data set {3, 5, 5, 7, 10}.
Find the median of the data set {12, 4, 8, 20, 6}.
practice.explain: Sorted: {4, 6, 8, 12, 20}. The middle (third) value is 8.

practice.q: A town's population dropped from 5,000 to 4,250. What is the percent decrease?
practice.explain: Change = 5000 - 4250 = 750. Percent decrease = 750 / 5000 x 100 = 15%.

practice.q: A bar graph's y-axis starts at 50 instead of 0. What is the main risk of reading it quickly?
choices: The data values themselves become inaccurate
Differences between bars can look much larger than they actually are
The x-axis labels become invalid
The graph can no longer show a trend
practice.explain: A truncated y-axis (not starting at zero) exaggerates the visual difference between bars even though the underlying data and their true proportional differences haven't changed.

lessons.title: Science and Data Reasoning on the ACT and ASVAB
lessons.intro: The ACT's optional Science section and the ASVAB's General Science subtest don't mainly test memorized facts, they test whether you can read an experiment's setup, a data table, or a conflicting-viewpoints passage and reason through it under time pressure.

sections.heading: Reading Experimental Setups
body: Most science-reasoning passages describe an experiment: what was varied (the independent variable), what was measured (the dependent variable), and what was held constant (controls). Before reading any question, quickly identify these three things, many questions are really just asking you to trace what happened to the dependent variable as the independent variable changed, which is a graph-reading task in disguise.

When a passage presents multiple trials or multiple scientists' conflicting viewpoints, resist the urge to fully understand every detail of each viewpoint. Instead, identify what each viewpoint agrees on and specifically where they disagree, a large share of conflicting-viewpoints questions test exactly that point of disagreement, not the full argument.

sections.heading: General Science Content Knowledge (ASVAB)
body: Unlike the ACT's Science section, the ASVAB's General Science subtest does test direct recall of basic facts across biology, chemistry, physics, and earth science, things like the function of red blood cells (carrying oxygen), Newton's laws of motion, or the water cycle's stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation). There's no passage to reason from; you either know the fact or you don't.

Because this section rewards raw recall, the highest-value prep is reviewing a compact list of core facts across the four science areas rather than rereading a full textbook, basic cell structures, the periodic table's major trends, simple machines, and the layers of the atmosphere cover a large share of what's actually asked.

keyTerms.def: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes; the dependent variable is what's measured in response.
Conditions held constant across an experiment so that only the independent variable's effect is being tested.
A science-reasoning format presenting multiple scientists' differing explanations for the same observation, tested on where they specifically agree or disagree.

practice.q: In an experiment testing how fertilizer amount affects plant height, what is the independent variable?
choices: Plant height
Amount of fertilizer
Type of soil (held constant)
Room temperature (held constant)
practice.explain: The independent variable is what the experimenter deliberately changes, here, the amount of fertilizer. Plant height is the dependent variable (what's measured in response).

practice.q: Two scientists agree that a lake's fish population declined but disagree on the cause, one blames pollution, the other blames overfishing. A question asks what the two views have in common. What should you look for?
choices: Which scientist is more likely correct
The specific shared claim both viewpoints accept (the decline itself), separate from their disagreement about cause
Additional data neither scientist mentioned
A vote on which theory is more popular
practice.explain: Conflicting-viewpoints questions often ask specifically what's shared versus what's disputed, both agree fish declined; they disagree only on why.

practice.q: Which fact is most likely tested directly (without a passage) on the ASVAB's General Science subtest?
choices: Interpreting a graph from a novel experiment
That red blood cells primarily function to carry oxygen
Evaluating two scientists' conflicting hypotheses
Reading a data table from an unfamiliar study
practice.explain: General Science tests direct recall of established facts (like red blood cell function), unlike the ACT Science section, which mainly tests reasoning from a given passage or data set rather than memorized content.

units.title: ASVAB Specialty Sections and Test-Day Strategy
units.summary: The ASVAB's mechanical and electronics subtests, how the AFQT score is actually calculated, and the logistics and anxiety-management skills that protect your score on test day.

lessons.title: Mechanical Comprehension and Electronics Information
lessons.intro: These two ASVAB subtests don't appear on the SAT or ACT at all, and they're exactly where students who only prepped for a college-admissions test get caught off guard, they test physical intuition and basic electrical concepts, not algebra.

sections.heading: Mechanical Comprehension: Levers, Gears, and Pulleys
body: A lever's mechanical advantage depends on where the fulcrum sits relative to the applied force (effort) and the resistance (load): moving the fulcrum closer to the load makes it easier to lift with less effort, but you must push the effort side a longer distance to compensate. Two meshed gears turn in opposite directions, and a smaller gear driven by a larger one spins faster but with less torque, the trade-off between speed and force is the core idea tested repeatedly.

In a pulley system, each additional supporting rope segment reduces the effort force needed to lift a load by roughly that same factor, at the cost of pulling a proportionally longer length of rope. Questions rarely require calculation; they mostly test whether you recognize which direction something moves, spins, or which side takes more force, based on a diagram.

sections.heading: Electronics Information: Basic Concepts
body: Voltage is the electrical pressure pushing current through a circuit, current is the actual flow of charge, and resistance opposes that flow, Ohm's law, V = I x R, ties all three together. In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component in sequence, so if one bulb burns out, the whole circuit breaks; in a parallel circuit, each branch has its own path, so one component failing doesn't necessarily stop current to the others.

A basic conductor (like copper) allows current to flow easily, while an insulator (like rubber or plastic) resists it, which is why wires are copper with a rubber or plastic coating. Common ASVAB questions ask you to identify a component from a simple symbol (like a battery, resistor, or switch) or to reason through what happens in a circuit if a specific part fails.

keyTerms.def: The trade-off a simple machine (lever, pulley, gear) provides between the force needed and the distance or speed required to apply it.
V = I x R, relating voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit.
In series, components share a single path (one failure breaks the circuit); in parallel, each component has an independent path.

practice.q: Moving a lever's fulcrum closer to the load has what effect?
choices: It requires more effort force but less distance
It requires less effort force but a longer effort-side distance
It has no effect on the force needed
It reverses the direction the load moves
practice.explain: Moving the fulcrum closer to the load increases mechanical advantage, reducing the effort force needed, but the trade-off is pushing the effort side through a longer distance.

practice.q: In a series circuit with three light bulbs, one bulb burns out. What happens to the other two?
choices: They stay lit, since each has its own path
They also go dark, since the single path is broken
They get brighter to compensate
It depends on the voltage of the battery
practice.explain: In a series circuit, all components share one path, breaking it anywhere (like a burnt-out bulb) stops current everywhere in the circuit, so all three bulbs go dark.

practice.q: Using Ohm's law, if a circuit has a resistance of 5 ohms and a current of 2 amps, what is the voltage?
choices: 2.5 volts
7 volts
10 volts
0.4 volts
practice.explain: V = I x R = 2 x 5 = 10 volts.

lessons.title: The AFQT Score and Building a Study Plan
lessons.intro: Your AFQT percentile decides whether you can enlist at all, and it's calculated from a specific formula, knowing that formula tells you exactly which four subtests deserve the bulk of your ASVAB study time.

sections.heading: How the AFQT Is Calculated
body: The AFQT (Armed Forces Qualification Test) score comes from just four of the ASVAB's subtests: Arithmetic Reasoning (AR), Mathematics Knowledge (MK), Word Knowledge (WK), and Paragraph Comprehension (PC). Word Knowledge and Paragraph Comprehension first combine into a single Verbal Expression (VE) score, and the AFQT raw score is calculated as 2xVE + AR + MK.

That raw score is then converted to a percentile from 1 to 99 using an official reference table, comparing your performance to a nationally representative sample, it's not a simple linear scale, so a specific raw score can't be converted to a percentile without that table. What matters practically is that the four subtests feeding into AFQT (AR, MK, WK, PC) deserve more study time than the other subtests if enlistment eligibility is your main goal.

sections.heading: Building a Study Plan Around Your Target
body: Start by taking a full practice test under real time limits to find your baseline, then compare that baseline to the specific score you need, a minimum AFQT percentile for enlistment eligibility, a specific line-score composite for a job you want, or a target SAT/ACT score for a college's typical admitted range. The gap between baseline and target tells you how many weeks of focused practice you realistically need, rather than guessing.

A study plan works best organized around two to three focus areas per week rather than randomly reviewing whatever feels most urgent that day, for instance, one week on linear equations and percentages, the next on reading structure and evidence, using timed practice sets to measure whether the specific gap is closing, not just whether you feel more prepared.

keyTerms.def: Calculated as 2xVE + AR + MK, using Verbal Expression, Arithmetic Reasoning, and Mathematics Knowledge subtest scores.
A combined score derived from the Word Knowledge and Paragraph Comprehension subtests.
A full-length, timed practice test taken early in prep to measure your current score gap against your target.

practice.q: Which four ASVAB subtests feed into the AFQT score?
choices: General Science, Mechanical Comprehension, AR, MK
Arithmetic Reasoning, Mathematics Knowledge, Word Knowledge, Paragraph Comprehension
Electronics Information, Auto Information, WK, PC
AR, MK, and two subtests of the student's choosing
practice.explain: The AFQT is built specifically from Arithmetic Reasoning, Mathematics Knowledge, Word Knowledge, and Paragraph Comprehension (the latter two combined into a Verbal Expression score).

practice.q: Why can't a raw AFQT score be converted to a percentile using simple math?
choices: The AFQT doesn't actually use percentiles
It's converted using an official reference table comparing you to a national sample, not a linear formula
Percentiles are only used for the SAT and ACT
The conversion changes every single test administration
practice.explain: The raw score (2xVE + AR + MK) is mapped to a 1-99 percentile through an official normed table, not a simple proportional calculation.

practice.q: What's the main advantage of taking a baseline practice test before building a study schedule?
choices: It replaces the need to take the real test
It tells you the specific gap between your current score and your target, so you know how much time you actually need
It guarantees a higher score on test day
It only matters for the ASVAB, not the SAT or ACT
practice.explain: A baseline turns 'I should study more' into a measurable gap, which lets you plan realistic timing and focus areas instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Test Day: Logistics, Scores, and Managing Anxiety
lessons.intro: The best preparation can still go sideways if you show up to the wrong room, forgot your ID, or spend the first ten minutes of the test in a panic spiral, test-day logistics and nerves deserve their own preparation, separate from content review.

sections.heading: Logistics You Should Lock Down Early
body: Confirm your test format (in-person or digital), location, and start time at least a week ahead, and check exactly what identification and materials are required, most testing centers require a valid photo ID matching your registration name exactly, and policies on calculators, phones, and scratch paper vary by test and by testing center. Arriving with the wrong ID or an unapproved calculator can mean not being allowed to test at all, regardless of how well you prepared.

For a digital test, confirm ahead of time whether it runs on your own device or a center-provided one, and if it's your device, test the required software or app the day before, not the morning of. For the ASVAB specifically, know whether you're taking it at a Military Entrance Processing Station (MEPS) or a satellite testing location, since arrival procedures and what to bring can differ between them.

sections.heading: Managing Test Anxiety in the Moment
body: A short surge of nervousness before a big test is normal and doesn't mean you're unprepared, the problem is when it escalates into racing thoughts that make you reread the same question three times without absorbing it. A concrete reset is slow, deliberate breathing: inhale for four counts, hold for four, exhale for four, repeated three or four times, which calms the physical stress response faster than trying to think calm directly.

If you hit a question that spikes anxiety specifically because you don't know it, flag it and move on immediately rather than staying stuck, a stalled five minutes on one hard question, while the clock burns down on easier ones you could have answered, is a bigger score risk than skipping that one question entirely. Come back to it only if time remains at the end.

keyTerms.def: Rules on accepted ID, calculators, and materials that vary by test and location and must be confirmed in advance.
A calming technique (inhale, hold, exhale, hold, each for a fixed count) used to reduce acute test anxiety.
Flagging a question that's causing a stall and moving on immediately, returning to it only if time remains.

practice.q: A student arrives at a testing center with a driver's license that has a different last name than their test registration (due to a recent name change not yet updated). What is the most likely outcome?
choices: No issue, since the ID is clearly the same person
The center may deny entry until the ID and registration match
The student is simply given a different test
This has no bearing on testing center policy
practice.explain: Testing centers generally require ID to exactly match registration; a mismatch (like an unupdated legal name) can result in being turned away, which is why confirming ID requirements in advance matters.

practice.q: Why is box breathing useful during a testing anxiety spike?
choices: It skips the need to answer harder questions
It calms the physical stress response through controlled breathing rather than through willpower alone
It's a required part of the test
It only works before the test starts, not during it
practice.explain: Slow, structured breathing directly affects the body's physical stress response, which is often faster and more reliable in the moment than simply trying to think your way out of panic.

practice.q: A student spends 6 minutes stuck on one hard question with 20 minutes left and 15 questions remaining. What's the best move?
choices: Keep working the hard question until it's solved, however long that takes
Flag it, move on to the remaining questions, and return only if time allows
Skip the rest of the section entirely
Guess immediately on every remaining question without reading them
practice.explain: Strategic skipping protects the many easier questions still available in the remaining time; a single hard question isn't worth risking the rest of the section.
